q: The law "Stress is proportional to strain within certain limits" is formulated by
explanation: Hooke's Law states stress ∝ strain within the elastic limit.

q: According to Hooke's law which one is correct?
explanation: Hooke's Law: stress = Modulus of Elasticity × strain, i.e. σ = Eε.

q: The zone between elastic limit and proportional limit on the elastic curve of an elastic material is known as
explanation: Beyond the proportional limit but still within the elastic limit, stress-strain is no longer linear — this is the non-linear elastic zone.

q: As per elastic theory of design the factor of safety is the ratio of
options: ultimate load to load at yield
explanation: Factor of safety (elastic design) = yield stress / working (permissible) stress.

q: Which of the following gives Poisson's ratio?
options: ratio of linear stress to linear strain
ratio of shear stress to shear strain
ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain
explanation: Poisson's ratio μ = lateral strain / longitudinal strain.

q: The value of Poisson's ratio always remains
explanation: For all real engineering materials, Poisson's ratio lies between 0 and 0.5, always less than one.

q: Normally the numerical value of Poisson's ratio is
explanation: Typical values: steel ≈ 0.3, concrete ≈ 0.15.

q: If the Poisson's ratio of a material is 0.25, the ratio of Modulus of Rigidity to the Young's Modulus is
The actual breaking stress of a ductile material from a tension test will be
options: less than the ultimate strength but greater than nominal breaking stress
explanation: True (actual) stress is computed on the reduced necked area, so it exceeds the nominal ultimate strength (computed on original area).

q: The product EI is called
explanation: E (Young's modulus) × I (moment of inertia) = flexural rigidity, a measure of resistance to bending.

q: The phenomenon of decreased resistance of material due to reversal of stress is called
explanation: Repeated/reversed stress cycles progressively weaken a material — this is fatigue.

q: The property of a material by which a body returns to its original shape after removal of the force, is called
explanation: Elasticity is the ability to recover original shape/size after unloading.

q: A perfectly elastic body is
options: that body which recovers its original shape completely after removal of force
a body of such a material with a lot of extensibility
a body made of rubber only
a body whose cross sectional dimensions are very small
explanation: By definition, perfect elasticity means complete shape recovery on unloading, regardless of material or size.

q: Load required to produce unit deflection is called
explanation: Stiffness = load / deflection, i.e. the load needed to produce one unit of deflection.

q: The property of material by which it can be drawn, due to tension, to a smaller section, is called
explanation: Ductility is the ability to be drawn into a wire/smaller section under tensile load.

q: Which of the following is a relatively ductile material?
explanation: Mild steel shows large plastic elongation before fracture, making it relatively ductile compared to the brittle options listed.

q: Toughness is
options: ability to absorb energy during plastic deformation
explanation: Toughness is the total energy a material can absorb before fracture, largely through plastic deformation.

q: The impact tests are used to determine
explanation: Impact tests (e.g. Izod/Charpy) measure the energy absorbed on sudden loading — i.e. toughness.

q: The property of material by which it can be beaten or rolled into plates, is called
explanation: Malleability is the ability to be hammered/rolled into thin sheets.

q: A member which is subjected to reversible tensile or compressible stress may fail at a stress lower than the ultimate stress of the material. The property of metal, is called
explanation: Failure under repeated/reversed stress below the ultimate stress is the fatigue phenomenon.

q: The safe value of stress below which the material will not fail when subjected to reversal of stress is known as
explanation: The endurance limit is the stress amplitude below which a material can withstand infinite stress reversals.

q: The method of increasing fatigue resistance by over stressing the metal by successively increasing the loading is known as
explanation: Coaxing improves fatigue strength by applying gradually increasing sub-critical stress cycles.

q: The phenomenon of slow growth of strain under a steady tensile stress, i.e. increasing with time, is called
explanation: Creep is time-dependent strain growth under sustained stress.

q: Permanent set is
options: the force which acts permanently on the body
the shape of the member just after completion of construction
ratio of poisson's ratio to young's modulus
explanation: Permanent set is the residual (irrecoverable) deformation left after unloading beyond the elastic limit.

q: If the value of Young's Modulus of elasticity for a material is zero, it implies that the material is
explanation: Zero stiffness against elastic deformation implies the material deforms permanently/plastically under any stress.

q: Limit of proportionality depends upon
explanation: The proportional limit is a material property, varying with the type of material.

q: The S.I. unit of modulus of elasticity is
explanation: Modulus of elasticity has units of stress (force/area); the SI unit is N/m² (Pascal).

q: Which of the following is dimensionless?
explanation: Strain is a ratio of length change to original length — dimensionless.

q: The stress at which extension of a material takes place more quickly as compared to the increase in load, is called
explanation: At the yield point, strain increases disproportionately for a small increase in load.

q: What is tenacity?
explanation: Tenacity refers to the ultimate tensile strength of a material.

q: Which of the following gives Modulus of Elasticity?
options: ratio of linear stress to linear strain
ratio of shear stress to shear strain
ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain
explanation: Young's Modulus (E) = linear stress / linear strain.

q: The Young's Modulus of elasticity is defined as a ratio of stress & strain within the
explanation: Hooke's Law (and hence E) is valid only within the elastic limit.

q: Which of the following gives Modulus of Rigidity?
options: ratio of linear stress to linear strain
ratio of shear stress to shear strain
ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain
explanation: Modulus of Rigidity (N/G) = shear stress / shear strain.

q: Which of the following gives Bulk Modulus?
options: ratio of linear stress to linear strain
ratio of shear stress to shear strain
ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain
ratio of the normal stress of equal magnitude on all six faces on a solid cube to the volumetric strain
explanation: Bulk Modulus (K) = uniform normal stress / volumetric strain.

q: Identify the correct relationship that exists among the modulus of elasticity (E), modulus of rigidity (N) and bulk modulus (k)
explanation: Standard elastic-constants relation: E = 9KN / (3K + N).

q: Normal strain is defined as
options: strain that is normal to shear strain
explanation: Normal (linear) strain = change in length / original length.

q: Shear strain is defined as
options: change in angle between planes at right angles
change in angles between two angles
explanation: Shear strain is the change in the right angle between two originally perpendicular planes/lines.

q: The modular ratio of two materials is defined as (E1 and E2 are the modulus of elasticity of the respective materials)
explanation: Modular ratio m = E1/E2, used in composite-section analysis (e.g. RCC transformed sections).

q: How does Young's Modulus vary with increase in temperature?
explanation: Interatomic bonding weakens with rising temperature, reducing stiffness (E) for most materials.

q: Which of the following materials will have the highest Young's Modulus?
explanation: Among these, mild steel has the highest stiffness (E ≈ 200 GPa).

q: What is strain energy?
options: energy that is spent for straining a body
energy stored in a body because of being strained
explanation: Strain energy is the elastic energy stored within a body as a result of deformation.

q: Strain energy of a member may be defined as work done on it
explanation: Strain energy equals the work done by external loads in deforming the member (stored internally).

q: The strain energy stored by a member when strained within elastic limit, is known as
explanation: Resilience is the strain energy stored (and recoverable) within the elastic range.

q: Proof resilience is the greatest stored energy at
explanation: Proof resilience is the maximum strain energy a material can absorb without permanent deformation, i.e. up to the elastic limit.

q: The stress in a member subjected to a force is
options: the resistance offered by the material per unit area to a force
explanation: Stress is the internal resisting force per unit area developed in response to an applied load.

q: The stress due to temperature change in a member depends on
explanation: Thermal stress only develops if expansion/contraction is restrained — hence it depends on the end/support conditions, not on cross-section or length directly.

q: The stress necessary to initiate yielding, is considerably
options: more than necessary to continue it
less than necessary to continue it
more than necessary to stop it
less than necessary to continue it
explanation: The upper yield point stress needed to start yielding is higher than the (lower) stress needed to continue/sustain plastic flow.

q: The ratio of intensity of stress in a case of a suddenly applied load to that of a gradually applied load is
explanation: A suddenly applied load produces twice the stress/deflection of the same load applied gradually.

q: The stress at which extension of a material takes place more quickly as compared to the increase in load, is called
explanation: This describes the yield point, where strain grows disproportionately fast relative to load.

q: When equal and opposite forces applied to a body tend to elongate it, the stress produced is called
explanation: Forces that pull a body apart (elongating it) produce tensile stress.

q: The bending moment acting on the plane of an element will cause the following type of stress on the plane
explanation: Bending moment produces normal (bending) stress that varies linearly across the section — tension on one side, compression on the other.

q: As the elastic limit reaches, tensile strain
options: decreases in proportion to the stress
increases in proportion to the stress
explanation: As per the answer key for this set; near the elastic limit the linear stress–strain proportionality begins to break down.

q: The ratio of elongations of a conical bar due to its own weight and that of a prismatic bar of the same length is
explanation: A conical bar under self-weight elongates only 1/3 as much as a prismatic bar of the same length and weight, due to the tapering cross-section.
